narrative:
The model predicted a 51% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven by three key factors, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year in law school was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile—far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students—signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your peers as the coursework became more demanding.

Next, your family income bracket worked in your favor. Being in the Low income group actually pulled the prediction slightly toward passing, because students from similar backgrounds in the data sometimes outperformed expectations.

Your first-year class rank was the third most important factor and again pushed strongly toward failure. Like your third-year rank, you placed in the lowest decile, well below the average sixth-decile performance of admitted students.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing in law school as the dominant signal that you were at elevated risk of failing the bar, outweighing the modest positive effect of your background and your solid but below-average LSAT and undergraduate GPA.

What you should do next is straightforward: focus on improving your study methods and time management so you can raise your class rank in the remaining years. Many students in your position have gone on to pass the bar after targeted academic recovery. Consider working with your school’s academic support office to build a concrete plan before reapplying.
